h1: The 7 Best Universal Remotes to Replace a Lost or Broken Clicker, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 universal remotes scored on device count, setup method, big buttons, backlighting, rechargeability and brand coverage.
summary: The One for All URC7880 is the universal remote to buy if you run several devices, since it controls 8 of them and has a learning feature for gear missing from its code list. The GE Rechargeable is the best pick for avoiding batteries, the UltraPro has the simplest pairing, and the RCA big-button models suit anyone who struggles with tiny keys.
intro: The costly mistake with universal remotes is buying on the promise of works with everything. No remote works with everything, and a model aimed at one TV brand can be a poor fit for a soundbar or streaming box. The real question is how many devices you want to control, and how the remote learns each one.

This ranking compares seven remotes on device count, setup method, button size and power source. We reviewed the spec sheets and listings, and we avoid claiming that any remote will pair with a specific model, because that depends on the code list for your exact brand. Always check compatibility for your own TV before ordering.

products.name: One for All URC7880 Universal Smart Remote
products.verdict: Eight devices, a learning feature and a setup app make it the most capable remote here.
products.description:
The URC7880 controls up to 8 devices, adds a learning feature and offers a setup app. It sits in the $25 to $50 bucket, a step above the basic remotes that cost under $25.

The learning feature is what puts it on top. Remotes usually rely on a built-in code database, and if your device is missing from it, you are stuck. A learning remote can copy a button from the original clicker, so an unusual soundbar or older player is not a dealbreaker. The setup app also cuts down on typing four-digit codes by hand. The tradeoff is complexity: more buttons and more options mean a longer first setup than a three-device remote.

Buy it if your living room has a TV, a box, a soundbar and more. Skip it if you only want one simple replacement.
pros: Covers gear outside the code database
cons: Longer first setup than basic remotes
products.idealFor: Living rooms with several devices that need one remote.
products.skipIf: You only need a simple replacement for one TV.

products.name: GE Rechargeable TV Remote Control
products.verdict: A backlit universal remote you charge instead of feeding with AAA cells.
products.description:
This GE remote is rechargeable and backlit, and it works as a universal replacement. It sits under $25. The main draw is dropping disposable batteries, which is more useful than it sounds because a remote is one of the most battery-hungry devices in a living room.

It takes second place because charging solves a daily irritation while the backlight makes it usable in a dim room. Against the URC7880 it controls fewer devices as far as the listing says, so it is a better fit for a main TV than a full home theater. The compromise with any rechargeable remote is that a flat battery leaves you without a remote until it is charged, so keep the cable where you can find it.

Choose it if you hate swapping batteries and mainly control a television. Skip it if you would rather pop in AAA cells from a drawer.
pros: Backlit keys help in dark rooms
products.idealFor: Anyone tired of replacing remote batteries.
products.skipIf: You prefer a remote you can fix with spare AAAs.

products.name: UltraPro Backlit OneTouch Universal Remote Control
products.verdict: OneTouch pairing and a backlit keypad for the simplest possible replacement TV remote.
products.description:
The UltraPro is a backlit replacement TV remote with OneTouch setup. It is in the under $25 bucket, and it is aimed at buyers who want to pair a remote with as little fuss as possible.

Its third position comes from simplicity. OneTouch setup is meant to replace the traditional routine of looking up brand codes and entering them one at a time, which is where many people give up. The backlight is a practical bonus. What it does not offer, based on the listing, is the multi-device reach or the learning ability of the One for All, so it is a TV remote first.

It suits a household member who just wants the TV to work again. Skip it if you plan to control a soundbar and a streaming box from the same remote.
cons: Mainly aimed at a single TV
products.idealFor: People who want a quick, no-fuss TV remote swap.
products.skipIf: You want to control several devices.

products.name: RCA Universal 4-Device Big Button Universal Remote
products.verdict: Four-device control with big buttons and support for streaming players.
products.description:
RCA's 4-device remote has large buttons and lists streaming support. It sits under $25. Four devices covers the usual set: a TV, a cable or streaming box, a soundbar and one more.

Fourth place reflects its balance. The big buttons make it much easier for older users or anyone who finds a dense keypad confusing, and streaming support is a practical addition now that many people watch through a box or stick rather than cable. It does not have a learning feature in the listing, so you rely on the code list for each brand.

Buy it if you want readable keys and more than one device. Skip it if you need to cover a wide array of equipment.
pros: Large buttons are easy to read
products.idealFor: Older users with a TV, box and soundbar.
products.skipIf: You own more than four controllable devices.

products.name: GE Big Button Universal Remote Control for Samsung
products.verdict: A big-button, multi-brand remote at the bottom of the price range.
products.description:
This GE remote pairs a big-button layout with multi-brand compatibility, at under $25. It is built for people who want clear, oversized keys and a straightforward replacement.

It sits fifth because the listing gives few details beyond the big buttons and the brand coverage. The Samsung mention suggests it is aimed at that brand, so check the compatibility list before buying for a different TV. It is a sensible, inexpensive way to give an older relative a more readable clicker without spending much.

Buy it if big buttons and the lowest cost matter most. Skip it if you need multiple devices, learning or backlighting.
pros: Oversized buttons are easy to press
products.idealFor: Budget big-button replacements for older users.
products.skipIf: You want backlighting or multi-device control.

products.name: RCA RCR313BE Big Button Three-Device Universal Remote
products.verdict: A three-device big-button remote for people who want less to learn.
products.description:
The RCR313BE controls three devices and has big buttons. It sits under $25. Three devices is the sweet spot for a plain TV, cable box and audio setup.

It ranks sixth because it is the older and simpler design of the RCA pair. You give up the fourth device and the streaming support mentioned on the 4-device model, in return for a slightly simpler layout and a lower price. For some households, fewer modes means fewer mistakes.

Choose it if three devices cover your living room. Skip it if you stream from a box and want the streaming-oriented 4-device version.
products.skipIf: You want streaming support or four devices.

products.name: GE Universal Remote Control for Samsung LG
products.verdict: A basic multi-brand replacement remote that covers popular TV makers.
products.description:
This GE universal remote lists multi-brand compatibility, including names such as Samsung and LG in its title, and sits under $25. It is a plain replacement, designed for the case where the original clicker is gone.

It comes last because it offers the fewest extras. There is no backlight, no learning feature and no device count in the listing. That does not make it a bad buy; for a single TV with a lost remote, it is often all you need. Just confirm that your TV brand and model family are covered before ordering.

Buy it if you need a cheap, broadly compatible stand-in. Skip it if you want features beyond the basics.
pros: Simple replacement for a lost remote
products.idealFor: A cheap stand-in for a lost TV remote.
products.skipIf: You want extras beyond basic control.

whatMatters.detail: A remote that controls three devices can run a TV, a box and an audio unit, while eight devices covers a full home theater. Buying more than you need adds complexity, and buying fewer leaves a second remote on the table. Count your devices and check the number on the listing.

A learning remote copies signals from your original remote, so gear missing from the built-in code list can still be controlled. It matters most with older equipment and niche soundbars. Look for the word learning in the listing, and keep the old remote until setup is finished.

Some remotes need you to look up a numeric code for each brand, while others use an app or a one-touch pairing step. Code entry is slow and easy to get wrong. Check the listing for app setup or OneTouch, and keep the code list handy if it is not offered.

Large keys help older users and anyone who finds small keypads frustrating. A backlight matters in a dark living room. Check the listing for big button or backlit, and compare the layout so the keys you use most are easy to find.

A universal remote is only universal within its code database. Remotes sold for Samsung or LG televisions may fit those brands best. Look up your TV model against the compatibility information on the listing and in the manual before buying.

faq.q: Will a universal remote work with my TV?
faq.a: It works if your TV brand is in the remote's code list or if the remote can learn from your old one. Check the compatibility notes on the listing and the manual. Brand names in a title are a hint, not a guarantee for every model.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying one?
faq.a: Assuming universal means every device. Always count the equipment you want to control and confirm the device count. Buying a three-device remote for a five-device setup leaves you with two remotes anyway.

faq.q: Is the One for All URC7880 worth over a cheaper remote?
faq.a: It is if you control several devices or own equipment that cheaper remotes cannot find in their lists. The learning feature and setup app justify the step up. For a single TV, the extra cost is not worth it.

faq.q: How do I set up a universal remote?
faq.a: Insert batteries or charge it, then follow the listed method: an app, OneTouch pairing or entering brand codes. Test power, volume and input for each device. Keep your old remote until you are sure everything works.
A rechargeable remote needs charging periodically, and how often depends on use. Keep the cable nearby. If you would rather not think about it, an AAA-powered model is the easier option.

faq.q: Can a universal remote control a streaming box?
faq.a: Some can, if the box uses infrared and is in the code list. The RCA 4-device model lists streaming support. Boxes that use Bluetooth or Wi-Fi remotes may not respond to an infrared universal remote.

finalTake: The One for All URC7880 is the best universal remote for anyone controlling several devices, thanks to its learning feature and 8-device reach. The GE Rechargeable is the choice for ditching batteries, and the UltraPro gives the easiest setup. For older users, the RCA big-button remotes are the safest bet.
